analysis.investment_thesis: Angel One is a well-known discount broker with a strong technology franchise, but the combination of a promoter holding of just 28.87%, borrowings that exploded from INR 1.2K Cr to INR 7.95K Cr in three years, chronically negative operating cash flows, and declining FY26 profits makes this a business I cannot own with conviction.
key_strengths: Strong technology platform and large retail customer base built over decades — real brand equity in discount broking
Historical profitability was excellent: net profit grew from INR 82 Cr (FY20) to INR 1,172 Cr (FY25)
Forward P/E of 20x is approaching reasonable if earnings stabilise — not egregiously priced by the market
key_risks: Borrowings have tripled to INR 7,951 Cr in FY26, pushing D/E to 0.76 — far above my 0.3 hard limit, and this trend is accelerating
Operating cash flow was negative INR 4,142 Cr in FY26 and negative in 3 of last 5 years — the business is consuming cash, not generating it
Net profit declined from INR 1,172 Cr (FY25) to INR 915 Cr (FY26) while revenue stagnated — SEBI F&O rule changes are biting
red_flags: Promoter holding at 28.87% is deeply below my 55% floor — I need to see a committed long-term owner behind a financial services business
Finance costs surged from INR 137 Cr (FY24) to INR 437 Cr (FY26) — the margin lending book is being funded expensively
Revenue stagnation (INR 5,239 Cr in FY25 to INR 5,137 Cr in FY26) combined with rising costs signals a business at peak cycle
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The broking business is inherently tied to market activity cycles — the extraordinary FY21–FY25 growth was driven by a bull market and retail participation surge. Now, with SEBI curbing F&O volumes and market breadth narrowing, FY26 shows the first cracks: flat revenue, rising debt costs, and a 22% drop in net profit. The explosion of borrowings from INR 788 Cr (FY23) to INR 7,951 Cr (FY26) reflects aggressive margin book expansion — a strategy that works beautifully in bull markets and fails badly in downturns.

I have seen this pattern in financial services: growth-at-any-cost through leverage ends in painful corrections. For me to own a financial services business, I need the promoter deeply committed (28.87% says otherwise), the balance sheet conservative (0.76 D/E says otherwise), and earnings stable (declining in FY26 says otherwise). Three strikes — avoid.
